lines: Build a real log with two transactions: one commits, one never does.
Run only the redo pass over it, before any undo at all.
Does redo apply the committed transaction's own updates, the uncommitted one's, or both?
answer: Redo doesn't know or care about commit status at all.

lines: Run it for real: redo genuinely reapplied the uncommitted transaction's own updates too, exactly like the committed one's.
Nothing about redo itself tells them apart.
steps.takeaway: Redo repeats history for everyone first; only the undo pass that follows tells a winner from a loser.

lines: A checkpoint recorded that one page was already safely on disk, with nothing else dirty at that moment.
Does redo, starting from that checkpoint's own bound instead of the very start of the log, still reach the correct final state?
answer: That bound is exactly how far back redo actually needs to look.

lines: Run it for real: redo starting from the checkpoint's own bound visited genuinely fewer log records, and reached the exact same final state as a full scan from the start.
steps.takeaway: A fuzzy checkpoint's own dirty-page bound lets redo skip what's already durable, without skipping anything it needs.

lines: Undo the uncommitted transaction's own last update, writing a compensation log record for it.
Now crash again, right there, in the middle of undoing.
On the next recovery, does undo repeat that same step, skip it, or resume exactly where it left off?
answer: The compensation log record already in the log says where.

lines: Run it for real: the second recovery resumed undo exactly where the first one left off.
The already-undone update got exactly one compensation log record, total, across both attempts.
steps.takeaway: A compensation log record bounds undo's own work across repeated failures: nothing already undone gets undone twice.

lines: The original paper behind this whole method names this kind of log record directly: a compensation log record.
Once that record undoes some earlier update, is its own effect ever itself undone later?
answer: A compensation log record is a redo-only log record.

lines: In that paper's own words: a compensation log record's own update is never undone, and such records are viewed as redo-only log records.
That same paper names the buffer policy this topic's own recovery assumes: letting an uncommitted page be written back early, and letting a committed one stay unwritten for a while.
Redo and undo together are exactly why that combination is safe: whatever was written back, and whenever, both passes can fix it up.
steps.takeaway: Steal and no-force are safe because redo and undo together can fix up a page however it was written back.

lines: So, pulling this topic together: one pass reconstructs the database's own state as of the crash, without asking yet who gets to keep their changes.
A separate bookkeeping record lets that pass start its work partway through the log instead of at the very beginning, with nothing lost by doing so.
Rolling back whoever didn't finish uses its own kind of record precisely so that trying again, after yet another failure, picks up exactly where it stopped rather than starting over.
And because both directions can always correct a page no matter when it reached disk, a system is free to write one back early or hold another back late, whichever happens to be faster.
